EM waves travel at 3.0×10^8 m/s in vacuum and can propagate through air, water, solids, or vacuum.
EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) is measured in decibels (dB), with 20 dB corresponding to 99% attenuation.
Far-field is defined as distances greater than λ/2π from the radiation source; near-field is less than λ/2π.
Wave impedance in air is approximately 377 Ω in far-field conditions.
The skin depth δ is inversely proportional to the square root of frequency, conductivity, and permeability.
For good conductors, reflection dominates EMI shielding, and multiple reflections are usually negligible.
Polymer/metallic filler composites face challenges in filler dispersion and weight increase.
Intrinsically conductive polymers like polypyrrole (PPY) and polyaniline (PANI) provide conductivity through doping.
PPY-coated PET fabric showed EMI SE of about 36 dB up to 1.5 GHz.
Carbon-based fillers with higher aspect ratios (SWCNTs) yield higher EMI shielding effectiveness than lower aspect ratio fillers (carbon black).
Magnetic fillers such as carbonyl iron and ferrites improve absorption-based shielding.
Electroless plating of nickel on MWCNTs increased EMI SE by 140% compared to pristine MWCNT composites.
Foams and aerogels reduce density and enhance absorption via wave scattering in pores.
Effective relative permittivity of composites can be approximated by Maxwell Garnett formula considering filler volume fraction.
Multiple reflections inside thin shields can significantly contribute to overall shielding effectiveness.
Reflection, absorption, and multiple reflections collectively determine total EMI shielding.
Conductive fillers create networks in polymers that enable interaction with incident EM waves.
Shielding by absorption increases with shield thickness and presence of electric/magnetic dipoles.
The ratio of shield thickness to skin depth (t/δ) influences the importance of multiple reflections.
Lightweight EMI shielding materials are critical for applications in aerospace and automotive industries.
